summary: Defines the Target-Dialog header field and the tdialog option tag for the Session Initiation Protocol. A request that creates a SIP dialog can use it to tell the recipient that the sender knows about an existing dialog with it. The recipient can use this to decide whether to authorize the request. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Before you knock on a door, you say which earlier conversation you are following up on. The person inside can then tell you really were part of it and let you in.

questions: how to authorize sip requests using dialog id
what is the sip target-dialog header
what is the tdialog option tag
how does sip authorize a refer request
subtitle: A SIP header that lets a request prove the sender knows about an existing dialog, so it can be authorized.

tldr.problem: A SIP user agent often must decide whether to accept a new dialog-creating request, such as a REFER for a call transfer, based on whether the sender is part of an existing dialog with it.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a Target-Dialog header field carrying the Call-ID, local tag and remote tag of that dialog, and the tdialog option tag signals support. The recipient checks the identifiers against its dialog.
tldr.outcome: The recipient can authorize the request outside the dialog without the problems of reusing the dialog. Security depends on the dialog using a sips URI and on cryptographically random identifiers.

today: RFC 4538 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It builds on RFC 3261.

sections.title: Why Dialog Awareness Matters
sections.content:
A SIP dialog is a persistent relationship between two user agents, created by requests such as INVITE, REFER and SUBSCRIBE. A user agent receiving such a request must decide whether to authorize it, and sometimes the right answer depends on whether the sender is in, or knows about, a dialog the recipient already has.

The RFC gives three examples. In call transfer, user agent A sends a REFER to B asking B to call C; B should accept it if B has an INVITE dialog with A. Existing implementations send the REFER inside the same dialog, which causes problems determining the dialog's lifecycle and which messages belong to which application usage. In the application interaction framework, a proxy sends a REFER to a user agent's GRUU. And an element on the INVITE path may send a SUBSCRIBE for the dialog event package to track the INVITE.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a person should only be allowed to ask you for something if they were already part of a conversation with you. This RFC gives them a way to show that they were.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
User agent A sends an INVITE to B through two servers acting as proxies. B answers with a 200 OK whose Supported header field includes the tdialog option tag, and the dialog is established.

Later, an entity that was on the request path, such as server A, sends a dialog-forming request like REFER to B. It addresses the request to the URI it learned from the Contact header field of the 200 OK. If that URI is a GRUU, the mechanism works across NAT boundaries. The request carries a Target-Dialog header field with the dialog identifiers: the Call-ID, local tag and remote tag.

B can then be certain the request came from A, the proxies, or someone they gave the identifiers to. This holds when the dialog was set up with a sips URI and the identifiers are cryptographically random, so nobody else could know them.
sections.eli5: Everyone on the original call knows its secret code. When someone shows up later quoting the code, the person who got the call knows they were really on it.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A UAC SHOULD include Target-Dialog when all four hold: the request is sent outside any existing dialog; the server may not authorize it unless the client proves awareness of a target dialog; the request has no other proof of that awareness; and the client knows the server supports the header. It can know this if it saw a Supported header with tdialog from the server within the target dialog. If that last condition fails, the client should not use this specification and should send within the existing dialog if it can.

The callid value MUST equal the target dialog's Call-ID. The remote-tag and local-tag parameters MUST be present, each given from the recipient's point of view. The request SHOULD also carry Require: tdialog, so a 403 can be told apart: either the server did not understand the header, or it understood it and still refused.

A UAS whose decision depends on dialog knowledge SHOULD check for the header. If the identifiers match an existing dialog set up with a sips URI, it SHOULD authorize whatever it would authorize for any entity on that dialog's path, or one trusted by such an entity. For a non-sips dialog it MAY do so, but authorization is optional because eavesdroppers could have the identifiers. If they do not match, or either tag is missing, the header MUST be ignored. Proxy behavior is unaffected.
sections.eli5: You only quote the code when you know the other side understands codes. The listener checks it against the real conversation and, if it matches, treats you like someone who was on the call.

sections.title: Header Field Definition and Extensibility
sections.content:
The Target-Dialog header field has the Call-ID followed by optional parameters: remote-tag, local-tag and generic parameters. It is allowed in INVITE, SUBSCRIBE and REFER requests, and proxies do not act on it.

Because the client must know in advance that the server supports it, user agents implementing this RFC should include a Supported header field in all dialog-forming requests and responses. RFC 3261 already makes that a SHOULD, and this RFC does not change it. Without tdialog in Supported, the extension is unlikely to be used, and the request will probably be resent within the existing dialog.
sections.eli5: The header is a little label on the request holding the conversation's ID and two names. Everyone must announce they understand labels, or nobody will use them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The scheme is only secure if two conditions hold. First, eavesdroppers must not see the dialog identifiers, which requires the original dialog to use a sips URI that provides TLS on each hop. Second, the identifiers must be unguessable. RFC 3261 requires a globally unique Call-ID and 32 bits of cryptographic randomness for each of the two tags, which the RFC judges adequate given a typical dialog lasts perhaps as long as a day.

It insists on true cryptographic randomness as set out in RFC 4086. Weaker pseudorandom identifiers are guessable, so an attacker could observe a sequence, guess the next one and use this mechanism to launch an attack.
sections.eli5: The secret code only works if nobody can listen in and nobody can guess it. So it must be sent over a protected line and be truly random.

sections.title: Difference from In-Reply-To
sections.content:
RFC 3261's In-Reply-To header field lists Call-IDs of calls the request references, to help build conversation threads in a user interface. The two header fields are not substitutes.

  • In-Reply-To is for a human or user interface; Target-Dialog is for the user agent itself, to authorize requests.
  • Target-Dialog refers to a specific dialog that must be currently in progress. In-Reply-To refers to a previous call attempt, probably one with no dialog, which is why it uses a Call-ID instead of a set of dialog identifiers.
  • In-Reply-To implies cause and effect; Target-Dialog only shows awareness.
sections.eli5: One label is a note for a person that says which earlier call this relates to. The other is a password check for the phone itself.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the Target-Dialog header field, which has no compact form. It also registers two header field parameters for it, local-tag and remote-tag, with no predefined values, under the process of RFC 3968.

It also registers the tdialog option tag. In a Require header it means the recipient must support the extension. In a Supported header it means the sender supports it.
sections.eli5: The new header, its two name tags and the option label are written into the official list so nobody else uses the same names.

data.title: Target-Dialog ABNF
data.code:
Target-Dialog  =  "Target-Dialog" HCOLON callid *(SEMI td-param)
td-param       =  remote-param / local-param / generic-param
remote-param   =  "remote-tag" EQUAL token
local-param    =  "local-tag" EQUAL token
